prov_muc_van.name: Mục Vân
prov_muc_van.lore: A small stretch of coastal grass and steppe around the racing track of Mục Vân Trang. Its people are grooms, riders and herders of the manor's spirit horses. An Earth vein under the pasture is said to be why the manor's foals run faster than any on the plain.

prov_p127.name: Điền Viên
prov_p127.lore: Forest and garden fields on the plain coast where Nhạn Thanh's scholars retire to farm. The village answers to Mục Vân Trang and lives by vegetables, orchards and letters written for herders. A quiet Wood vein under its orchards draws old scholars who have taken up cultivation late.

prov_p128.name: Yến Quy
prov_p128.lore: Grass and forest on the plain coast around the old farm where the swallows return each spring. Its farmers plant by the birds. A warm spring in the fields is where the swallows bathe before they nest.

prov_p129.name: Chu Tân
prov_p129.lore: Low wet grass and forest on a shore below the level of the high tide, round the old ford whose river has wandered away. The village answers to Mục Vân Trang and hauls travellers and herds across the tidal creek. A warm pool by the old ford is where the ferrymen thaw out after winter crossings.

prov_p130.name: Lô Cảng
prov_p130.lore: Grass and forest around the reed harbour where Lạc Hà keeps its western watch. Watchmen and fishers share the land and the tower lights a fire at strange sails. A hot spring inland warms the watchmen after their nights on the tower.

prov_p131.name: Diêm Điền
prov_p131.lore: Flat grass and forest along a coast of glittering salt pans, the oldest on the continent. Its people rake salt and sell it up and down the plain. On the shore lie the drowned walls of Triều Một Trấn, a town the sea took.

prov_p38.name: Nhạn Thanh
prov_p38.lore: Dry steppe and grass around Nhạn Thanh Thành, the wool market of the western plain, where a river meets the sea. Its herders drive their flocks to the city, and its lake is where the wild geese come down each autumn. On the steppe shore stands Nhạn Trận Môn, the gate that drills the plain's levies.

prov_p73.name: Thanh Điền
prov_p73.lore: Forest and fields so wide around Thanh Điền Trấn that its farmers ride to work. The town answers to Mục Vân Trang and holds a horse fair on the night its head was born. On the coast lie the ruins of Di Hà Trấn, a river town whose river left it.

prov_p74.name: Thảo Đường
prov_p74.lore: Farms, fish ponds and forest round Thảo Đường Thành, the granary of the western plain. Its people grow rice and hemp and raise fish and ducks in the grass-banked ponds. On the coast lies Dã Độ Trấn, the older ferry town that emptied when the city was built.

prov_p75.name: Ngư Lương
prov_p75.lore: Forest and grass where a plain river spills into the sea through the great zigzag weir. Its families keep the fish of their own stretch of weir. Upstream a white elm wood gives the timber for the weir's frames.

prov_r11_1.name: Vụ Vũ Lâm
prov_r11_1.lore: The wooded isle of Phù Chử Đảo, forest from shore to crown, ringed by a raft of wild ducks so thick the water looks feathered. No one lives here and no sect holds it; egg-gatherers row over from the plain coast each spring, wait for the ducks to part before landing, and take only a few eggs from each nest. The forest floor is soft with moulted down, which gives the wood its name.

prov_r11_10.name: Bạch Thảo
prov_r11_10.lore: Grass and dry steppe on the coast, rising to bare hills inland. Its herders run sheep on the pale autumn grass and fish the shore. A warm spring in the steppe is where the herds drink in winter.

prov_r11_11.name: Thanh Phong
prov_r11_11.lore: Wide grass and steppe on a low coast where the sea and the sky meet in one colour. Its town ships wool and hides along the plain coast. A Water vein near the shore is named for the old line about autumn water and the endless sky.

prov_r11_12.name: Song Tỉnh
prov_r11_12.lore: Dry inland steppe with patches of grass, far from any river or coast. Its herders live by two deep wells and move their flocks between them. An Earth vein under the open steppe draws Mục Vân's riders to cultivate on long journeys.

prov_r11_13.name: Vãn Chu
prov_r11_13.lore: Grass and steppe on the coast, with a few red badland gullies inland. Its fishers put out in the evening and come home singing in the dark. Black vultures nest on the high ground and follow the herds.

prov_r11_2.name: Mộ Cảnh Lĩnh
prov_r11_2.lore: The westernmost isles: the grassy hump of Tịch Chiếu Đảo with its stone bench and cairns, and a smoking volcanic cone of forest and bare rock farther out. No settlement has ever stood here; boats from the mainland bring Lạc Hà's dying elders to Tịch Chiếu and do not wait. The cone holds Hỏa Ngọc Mạch on Thúy Vi's sealed chart, and only that sect's short guarded voyages ever land on it.

prov_r11_3.name: Chung Phàm
prov_r11_3.lore: A small high spur of steppe and grass over the sea, the last stop for boats going out to the far west. Its little town sells water, salt fish and rope to the boats. Its people say they live at the edge of the world, and that the sunset is nearer to them than to anyone.

prov_r11_4.name: Bình Sa
prov_r11_4.lore: Grass and forest rising from level sands to high ground. Its villagers fish and herd on the shore flats. Wild stallions run on the uplands and are the terror of herders and the prize of Mục Vân's horse-breakers.

prov_r11_5.name: Hòa Lũng
prov_r11_5.lore: Wide coastal grass, mostly ploughed, with a little steppe and forest. Its farmers grow rice and millet on raised ridges against the floods. A Wood vein under the level grass makes the ridges green earlier than anywhere on the plain.

prov_r11_6.name: Thán Ổ
prov_r11_6.lore: Inland grass and steppe with woods in its hollows. Its villagers burn charcoal in the woods and sell it to the towns. On the steppe stand the empty halls of Phù Dao Quán, a school that ended after the cold year of 1120.

prov_r11_7.name: Di Tân
prov_r11_7.lore: Grass and forest rising from the coast to high wooded ground. Its town is a crowded harbour for the plain's coast boats. A Wood vein high in the forest draws Lạc Hà disciples, and on the shore lie the ruins of Ngư Hỏa Trấn, broken by the storm of 870.

prov_r11_8.name: Mục Địch
prov_r11_8.lore: Wide inland grass and steppe, the heart of the open plain. Its herders follow their flocks and call them with bamboo flutes. Grass wolves hunt the flocks in winter, and the herders sleep beside their sheep.

prov_r11_9.name: Phùng Nghênh
prov_r11_9.lore: Grass and steppe on the coast, with an Earth vein on the rise inland. Its town is known for its inns and its welcome to travellers from a thousand miles away. Herders say no stranger has ever slept outside in Phùng Nghênh.

prov_muc_van_spirit_vein_1.name: Trì Vân Mạch
prov_muc_van_spirit_vein_1.look: A low swell of pasture where the grass grows thick and silver-green and the spirit foals of Mục Vân graze in their first year.
prov_muc_van_spirit_vein_1.lore: An Earth vein runs under the pasture, and the manor says a foal raised on it never tires. Khấu Mục Vân lets only his own riders cultivate here, at dawn, among the horses.

prov_p127_spirit_vein_1.name: Ẩn Canh Mạch
prov_p127_spirit_vein_1.look: A small wood behind the scholars' gardens, its floor soft with leaf mould and a stone seat at its centre.
prov_p127_spirit_vein_1.lore: A Wood vein runs under the wood, gentle enough for those who come to cultivation late. Retired scholars of Nhạn Thanh sit here after their morning in the fields, and a few have reached Luyện Khí in old age.

prov_p128_hot_spring_1.name: Yến Ngữ Thang
prov_p128_hot_spring_1.look: A warm pool in the fields edged with reeds, crowded each spring with swallows dipping and calling.
prov_p128_hot_spring_1.lore: The swallows of Yến Quy bathe here before they nest. The farmers say a year when they bathe late is a year to plant carefully.

prov_p129_hot_spring_1.name: Ôn Tân Trì
prov_p129_hot_spring_1.look: A steaming pool on the wet shore beside the old ferry posts, lower than the sea at high tide but never flooded by it.
prov_p129_hot_spring_1.lore: The ferrymen of Chu Tân thaw out here after winter crossings. The tide rises all around it and stops at its rim, and no one knows why.

prov_p130_hot_spring_1.name: Hàn Thú Thang
prov_p130_hot_spring_1.look: A walled hot spring in the grass inland of the reed harbour, with a small guardroom beside it.
prov_p130_hot_spring_1.lore: Lạc Hà built the guardroom when it raised the western watch, so the watchmen could warm themselves after a night on the tower. A watchman who leaves his post for the spring is made to bathe in the sea instead.

prov_p131_hot_spring_1.name: Hàm Thủy Thang
prov_p131_hot_spring_1.look: A hot salty spring in the grass behind the salt pans, its rim crusted white.
prov_p131_hot_spring_1.lore: Its water is saltier than the sea, and the salt-makers once boiled it for salt in winter. Now they soak their aching backs in it after the summer raking.

prov_p131_ruin_2.name: Triều Một Trấn
prov_p131_ruin_2.look: Low broken walls standing in shallow water on the grassy shore, visible only at low tide.
prov_p131_ruin_2.lore: Salt traders built the town on the shore in 350, before any sect held the plain. In 988 a storm surge broke its sea wall and drowned the lower streets, and its people moved up the coast to Diêm Điền. At low tide the salt-makers still walk out to its gate.

prov_p38_lake_1.name: Lạc Nhạn Hồ
prov_p38_lake_1.look: A broad shallow lake in the grass with level sandy shores, covered each autumn with wild geese.
prov_p38_lake_1.lore: The geese that fly in formation over Nhạn Thanh come down here to rest each autumn. As in the city, no one may shoot a goose on the lake, and the herders say the geese know it.

prov_p38_minor_seat_p.name: Nhạn Trận Môn
prov_p38_minor_seat_p.look: A walled gate seat on the steppe shore, its parade ground marked with lines of white stones in the shape of a goose formation.
prov_p38_minor_seat_p.lore: Survivors of Chiết Kích Nguyên founded the gate in 806 under Lạc Hà Tông, swearing that Lạc Hà's disciples would never again fight in loose order. Its disciples drill in formations modelled on the flight of the wild geese, and every spring they drill the plain's levies. Their banner shows a goose formation breaking off at the cold.

sect.name: Nhạn Trận Môn
sect.craft: battle formations (chiến trận) for disciple squads; drills the plain's levies

prov_p73_spirit_vein_1.name: Thanh Miêu Mạch
prov_p73_spirit_vein_1.look: A wood of young trees among the fields, where the seedlings always sprout a fortnight before the rest.
prov_p73_spirit_vein_1.lore: A Wood vein runs under the wood, and the farmers of Thanh Điền bring their seed rice here to sprout. Mục Vân Trang lets them, as long as they keep their horses out.

prov_p73_ruin_2.name: Di Hà Trấn
prov_p73_ruin_2.look: A ring of grass-grown walls on the coast with a stone river quay that now faces a dry meadow.
prov_p73_ruin_2.lore: Boatmen built the town in 430 on the plain's widest river, the same river that once ran past Chu Tân's ford. The river wandered away over the years, and by 860 the quay faced only grass and the last boatmen had left. Herders now shelter their flocks in its walls.

prov_p74_forest_1.name: Bảo Thụ Lâm
prov_p74_forest_1.look: A wood of tall old trees between the fish ponds, their autumn leaves so bright they look lacquered.
prov_p74_forest_1.lore: The city's first farmers left the wood standing as a windbreak for the ponds. Families of Thảo Đường call a promising child a jewel tree after it, from the old saying.

prov_p74_ruin_2.name: Dã Độ Trấn
prov_p74_ruin_2.look: Roofless houses on the grassy shore beside a silted landing, where a rotten ferry boat lies across the mud.
prov_p74_ruin_2.lore: Ferrymen founded the town in 500 on the coast creek. When Thảo Đường Thành rose in 680 its trade drew the ferrymen away, the landing silted, and by 712 only the boat was left. The coast says the boat turns on its own when the tide comes in.

prov_p75_forest_1.name: Bạch Du Lâm
prov_p75_forest_1.look: A wood of pale-barked elms on the grass upstream of the weir, cut in rows and growing back in rows.
prov_p75_forest_1.lore: The fishers of Ngư Lương cut its elms for the weir's frames and replant one for each they fell. Each stretch of weir has its own rows of trees.

prov_r11_10_village_1.name: Bạch Thảo Thôn
prov_r11_10_village_1.look: A herding village on the steppe shore, its sheep pens of piled stone and the autumn grass around it bleached white.
prov_r11_10_village_1.lore: Its herders run sheep on the pale grass and fish the shore in winter. Their wool goes to Nhạn Thanh and is said to be the whitest on the plain.

prov_r11_10_hot_spring_2.name: Ẩm Câu Tuyền
prov_r11_10_hot_spring_2.look: A steaming spring in a dip of the steppe, its overflow running into a long stone trough.
prov_r11_10_hot_spring_2.lore: The herders water their flocks here in winter when the ponds freeze. Mục Vân's couriers always stop to water their horses, and the trough's stones are worn by hooves.

prov_r11_11_town_1.name: Thanh Phong Trấn
prov_r11_11_town_1.look: A small walled town on the steppe shore, its wool sheds open to the sea wind.
prov_r11_11_town_1.lore: The town ships wool and hides along the plain coast. Its name comes from the old line about clear breezes rising, and the merchants say the breeze keeps the moth out of their wool.

prov_r11_11_spirit_vein_2.name: Nhất Sắc Mạch
prov_r11_11_spirit_vein_2.look: A flat grassy shore where on calm evenings the sea and the sky turn the same colour and the horizon disappears.
prov_r11_11_spirit_vein_2.lore: A Water vein runs under the shore, named for the line in which the autumn water and the endless sky are one colour. Lạc Hà's disciples cultivate here at the hour of the evening glow.

prov_r11_12_village_1.name: Song Tỉnh Thôn
prov_r11_12_village_1.look: A cluster of felt tents and stone pens around two deep stone wells in the open grass.
prov_r11_12_village_1.lore: The herders move between the two wells with the seasons and never let one run dry. A quarrel over water here is settled by the oldest woman of the village.

prov_r11_12_spirit_vein_2.name: Khoáng Dã Mạch
prov_r11_12_spirit_vein_2.look: A bare rise in the steppe where the grass grows short and the ground hums faintly underfoot.
prov_r11_12_spirit_vein_2.lore: An Earth vein runs under the rise, steady and broad. Mục Vân's couriers break their journeys here to cultivate an hour before riding on.

prov_r11_13_village_1.name: Vãn Chu Thôn
prov_r11_13_village_1.look: A fishing village on the grassy coast where the boats put out at sunset, each with a lamp at the stern.
prov_r11_13_village_1.lore: Its fishers go out in the evening and come home singing in the dark, guided by the lamps. In 803 they stayed ashore, and they still stay ashore on that dusk every year.

prov_r11_13_beast_lair_2.name: Hắc Thứu Đài
prov_r11_13_beast_lair_2.look: A grassy terrace of high ground streaked white with droppings, where huge black birds sit hunched on the rocks.
prov_r11_13_beast_lair_2.lore: Spirit vultures nest here and take lambs and sick sheep from the herds. Herders say they gather over any flock that is about to suffer a loss, and drive their sheep home when they see them.

prov_r11_3_town_1.name: Chung Phàm Trấn
prov_r11_3_town_1.look: A small walled town on a high steppe spur over the sea, its water tanks cut into the rock.
prov_r11_3_town_1.lore: It is the last stop for boats going out to the far west, and it sells them water, salt fish and rope. Its people claim the sunset is nearer to them than to anyone on the continent.

prov_r11_4_village_1.name: Bình Sa Thôn
prov_r11_4_village_1.look: A village on flat sands at the shore, its houses raised on low mounds against the spring tides.
prov_r11_4_village_1.lore: Its villagers fish the shore flats and herd sheep on the grass behind. Geese come down on the level sand each autumn, and the village holds a feast when the first ones land.

prov_r11_4_beast_lair_2.name: Liệt Mã Cương
prov_r11_4_beast_lair_2.look: An open grassy ridge high above the coast, its turf torn by hooves.
prov_r11_4_beast_lair_2.lore: Wild spirit stallions run here and kill any horse that strays into their herd. Mục Vân's horse-breakers come each year to try to take one, and come back with fewer riders than they took.

prov_r11_5_village_1.name: Hòa Lũng Thôn
prov_r11_5_village_1.look: A farm village on the coastal grass, its fields raised on long ridges with ditches between.
prov_r11_5_village_1.lore: Its farmers grow rice and millet on ridges that stand above the floods. The village sends its grain by cart to Thảo Đường Thành.

prov_r11_5_spirit_vein_2.name: Bình Vu Mạch
prov_r11_5_spirit_vein_2.look: A wide patch of open grass that turns green weeks before the rest of the plain each spring.
prov_r11_5_spirit_vein_2.lore: A Wood vein runs under the level grass, gentle and wide. The farmers of Hòa Lũng plant first beside it and say the vein wakes the plain.

prov_r11_6_village_1.name: Thán Ổ Thôn
prov_r11_6_village_1.look: A village of black-roofed huts in a wooded hollow, its charcoal mounds smoking under turf.
prov_r11_6_village_1.lore: Its people burn charcoal in the woods and carry it to the towns of the plain. Each family has its own wood and cuts it in turn so the trees grow back.

prov_r11_6_spirit_vein_2.name: Thiên Cao Mạch
prov_r11_6_spirit_vein_2.look: A broad rise of steppe under an enormous sky, with a single stone cairn on its crown.
prov_r11_6_spirit_vein_2.lore: An Earth vein runs under the rise, named for the old line in which heaven is high and earth far-reaching. The disciples of Phù Dao Quán cultivated here, and their cairn still stands.

prov_r11_6_ruin_3.name: Phù Dao Quán
prov_r11_6_ruin_3.look: Empty halls of grey stone on the open steppe, their doors banging in the wind and the courtyard drifted with dust.
prov_r11_6_ruin_3.lore: A small school sworn to Lạc Hà Tông founded the abbey in 760 to cultivate on the open steppe. The cold year of 1120 killed its herds and its old master, and in 1121 its few disciples went to serve Mục Vân Trang. Herders shelter in its halls in storms.

prov_r11_7_town_1.name: Di Tân Trấn
prov_r11_7_town_1.look: A small walled harbour town on the grassy coast, its harbour so packed with coast boats that one can walk across it.
prov_r11_7_town_1.lore: Its name comes from the old line about boats crowding the ford. It is the busiest harbour on the plain coast after Nhạn Thanh, and its harbour master settles mooring quarrels by lot.

prov_r11_7_spirit_vein_2.name: Thanh Vân Mạch
prov_r11_7_spirit_vein_2.look: A high forest shoulder above the coast where the clouds come down through the trees.
prov_r11_7_spirit_vein_2.lore: A Wood vein runs under the forest, named for the old line about never letting the will for the blue clouds fall. Lạc Hà's young disciples are sent here to cultivate before their first trial.

prov_r11_7_ruin_3.name: Ngư Hỏa Trấn
prov_r11_7_ruin_3.look: A broken sea wall and roofless houses on a grassy shore, with rows of rusted lamp hooks along the old quay.
prov_r11_7_ruin_3.lore: Fishers built the town in 610, and its boats fished at night by lamplight. The great storm of 870 broke its sea wall and sank its fleet in the harbour, and the survivors moved to Di Tân. Fishers still see lights on the water off the old quay.

prov_r11_8_village_1.name: Mục Địch Thôn
prov_r11_8_village_1.look: A herding village of felt and timber on open grass, its flocks moving around it to the sound of bamboo flutes.
prov_r11_8_village_1.lore: Its herders call their flocks with flutes, each family with its own tune. A sheep that answers the wrong tune is given back without a word.

prov_r11_8_beast_lair_2.name: Thảo Lang Nguyên
prov_r11_8_beast_lair_2.look: Rolling high grass where the wind shows long tracks through the blades and old wolf dens open on the slopes.
prov_r11_8_beast_lair_2.lore: Spirit wolves the colour of dry grass hunt here and are hard to see until they move. In winter they come down on the flocks, and the herders sleep beside their sheep with fire pots.

prov_r11_9_town_1.name: Phùng Nghênh Trấn
prov_r11_9_town_1.look: A small walled town on the grassy coast whose main street is nothing but inns, each with a lantern at the door.
prov_r11_9_town_1.lore: Its name comes from the old line about welcomes from a thousand miles away. The town's custom is that no stranger sleeps outside, and the innkeepers take turns to house those who cannot pay.

prov_r11_9_spirit_vein_2.name: Trường Phong Mạch
prov_r11_9_spirit_vein_2.look: An open grassy rise inland of the town where the wind never stops and the grass lies flat.
prov_r11_9_spirit_vein_2.lore: An Earth vein runs under the rise, and the wind over it is said to carry the qi far across the plain. Travellers staying at Phùng Nghênh come up to cultivate before setting out.
